intro: The circus arrived overnight in a town that isn't on any map, its big top stitched from canvas the colour of old thunder. Admission is free, but the ticket-taker only lets you in if you can read your ticket, and every ticket is written in a different hand, some in ink that vanishes by dawn. Inside, the performers move through their routines as though rehearsed for someone else's audience, and at the centre of the ring stands a great oak dressing-case with eight drawers, each one padded with velvet the shade of a circus performer's finest coat. The ringmaster says nothing about what belongs where, only that every act must fit its trunk exactly, and that a true professional never packs what doesn't belong. Between shows, the clowns keep a ledger of who was in and who was out, each name crossed and recrossed until the crossings themselves seem to form a pattern. No one has yet asked what the pattern means, but the acrobats whisper that the tent will fold itself up the night the last drawer clicks shut.
echo: The painted horses go up and down and round, and never get anywhere.

puzzles.title: The Flying Act
puzzles.flavor: A sensor that only knows up and down, six times over. Alpha and Omega traded places before this was written down.

hints: Write each number in binary. Six yes-or-no choices: is there an alphabet built from exactly that? And if what you get still isn't a word, reread the flavour text.
Braille: each bit is one of the six dots (1, 2, 4 down the left column; 8, 16, 32 down the right). Then one more layer: Turn the alphabet end to end: A for Z, B for Y.

puzzles.title: Strongman
puzzles.flavor: A strip of paper full of holes, seven across. A baker's dozen steps separate this from the truth, in either direction.

hints: Seven positions a row, each punched or not. What were seven bits once enough for? And if what you get still isn't a word, reread the flavour text.
Seven-bit ASCII: a hole is 1, the leftmost hole is the highest bit. Then one more layer: Shift every letter 13 places (A↔N).
